content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe where and how reabsorption occurs
Describe the adaptations of tubule cells for reabsorption

is the second stage of urine formation. Useful substances that were filtered are taken back into the blood. This happens mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule. The process is selective because only needed substances are reabsorbed.
The reabsorption of useful substances from the filtrate back into the blood
Most glucose, amino acids, salts, water
Na⁺/K⁺ pump creates sodium gradient (uses ATP)
Glucose moves into blood via facilitated diffusion
Water moves by osmosis into blood
Collecting duct: regulated amount (controlled by ADH)
Blood concentration above which a substance appears in urine
Above threshold: glucose appears in urine
Maximum rate at which a substance can be reabsorbed
Reabsorption is the opposite of filtration
Glucose in urine always means diabetes
Could indicate diabetes but needs proper diagnosis
About 50% of filtered urea is reabsorbed
Return of useful substances from filtrate to blood
Concentration above which substance appears in urine
Selective reabsorption returns useful substances to blood
Mainly occurs in proximal convoluted tubule
Glucose and amino acids: 100% reabsorbed by active transport
PCT cells adapted: microvilli, many mitochondria
Renal threshold: concentration above which substance appears in urine
~99% of filtrate reabsorbed; ~1-2 L becomes urine
